summary: Describes the SEED encryption algorithm, which is widely used in security systems in the Republic of Korea. It covers the encryption, the key scheduling, the S-boxes, and test vectors. It replaces RFC 4009. It is informational.

eli5.summary: SEED is a way of scrambling messages with a secret key, widely used in Korea. This memo explains the scrambling steps and gives sample answers to check your work.

subtitle: The 128-bit Korean national block cipher, specified with its round function, key schedule, S-boxes and test vectors.

tldr.problem: RFC 4009 described the SEED cipher, but its function and SS-box definitions were ambiguous, which hurt interoperable implementations.
tldr.mechanism: SEED is a 16-round Feistel cipher with a 128-bit block and a 128-bit key. Its round function uses two 8x8 S-boxes, XOR and modular addition, and a key schedule makes a pair of 32-bit subkeys per round.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4269 clarifies the definitions and pseudo code without changing the algorithm, and obsoletes RFC 4009. It is an Informational RFC.

today: RFC 4269 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 4009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What SEED Is and What Changed
sections.content:
SEED is a 128-bit symmetric key block cipher developed by KISA (Korea Information Security Agency) since 1998. The RFC says it is a national standard encryption algorithm in the Republic of Korea and has been widely used there for confidential services such as electronic commerce and financial services over wired and wireless communication.

Its listed features are a Feistel structure with 16 rounds, a 128-bit block, a 128-bit key, a round function designed to resist known attacks, two 8x8 S-boxes, and mixed XOR and modular addition.

RFC 4269 obsoletes RFC 4009. That document had cryptographically ambiguous function and SS-box definitions. This version corrects the definitions of R1', Z, X and the SS-boxes and adds more detailed pseudo code. The RFC states that the SEED algorithm itself has not been changed.
sections.eli5: SEED is a secret-code machine used a lot in Korea. This memo fixes confusing instructions in the old manual, but the machine works exactly as before.

sections.title: The Feistel Structure
sections.content:
A 128-bit input is split into two 64-bit halves, L (the most significant 64 bits) and R (the least significant). In each of the 16 rounds the right half goes into a round function F along with a 64-bit subkey Ki from the key schedule. The result is XORed into the left half and the halves swap roles. In the last round the halves are not swapped.

Because of this layout, decryption is the encryption algorithm run with the round subkeys in reverse order.

The notation used includes ^ for XOR, addition (+) and subtraction (−) modulo 232, || for concatenation, and circular rotations written << n and >> n.
sections.eli5: Imagine two piles of cards. Each round you scramble one pile using the other pile and a secret, then swap them. To unscramble, you do the same rounds in the opposite order.

sections.title: The Round Function F and Function G
sections.content:
The round function F takes a 64-bit block, splits it into two 32-bit halves R0 and R1, and mixes in the two 32-bit subkey blocks Ki0 and Ki1. It then applies three layers of the function G with additions to mix the two halves. The RFC gives the outputs R0' and R1' as nested expressions of G.

G has two layers: a layer of two 8x8 S-boxes, S0 and S1, and a permutation of sixteen 8-bit sub-blocks. It takes four 8-bit inputs X0 to X3 and produces Z0 to Z3 using the masks m0 = 0xFC, m1 = 0xF3, m2 = 0xCF and m3 = 0x3F.

For speed, four extended S-boxes SS0 to SS3 are defined (tabulated in Appendix A.2), so that Z = SS0(X0) ^ SS1(X1) ^ SS2(X2) ^ SS3(X3). This is faster but takes more memory.
sections.eli5: Inside each round the numbers are looked up in a scrambling table and stirred together with a few simple operations, like shuffling and mixing a deck over and over.

sections.title: The Key Schedule
sections.content:
The 128-bit key is divided into four 32-bit blocks Key0 to Key3. For each round i from 1 to 16 the schedule computes Ki0 = G(Key0 + Key2 - KCi) and Ki1 = G(Key1 - Key3 + KCi).

After odd rounds, Key0 || Key1 is rotated right by 8 bits. After even rounds, Key2 || Key3 is rotated left by 8 bits. The constants KC1 to KC16 are listed in a table, starting with KC1 = 0x9E3779B9.
sections.eli5: The secret key is turned into sixteen smaller keys, one per round, by twisting it a little each time so every round uses a different key.

sections.title: Object Identifiers, Security and Test Vectors
sections.content:
For protocols that negotiate algorithms, the RFC defines three object identifiers under the KISA arc. id-seedCBC is for SEED in CBC mode, with a 16-octet initialization vector as its parameter. id-seedMAC is for a MAC based on SEED, with the MAC length in bits. pbeWithSHA1AndSEED-CBC is for password-based encryption using SHA-1 and SEED, described in RFC 2898.

The Security Considerations section is a single statement: no security problem has been found on SEED, with pointers to an ISO/IEC document and a CRYPTREC evaluation report.

Appendix A gives the S-boxes S0 and S1 and the extended SS-boxes. Appendix B gives test vectors, each with a key, plaintext, ciphertext and the intermediate values of all 16 rounds, so implementers can check their work.
sections.eli5: The memo gives each flavor of SEED an official name tag so programs can say which they use, and includes worked answers so builders can check that their copy gets the same results.
